title: Paonia Well Depth and Drilling Cost Guide
meta_description: Paonia wells have a 67-foot median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $9,400-$17,000.
h1: What Paonia Wells Cost, Produce, and Require
intro_html:
Paonia sits in a productive but locally variable well area. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 67 feet and a median reported yield of 15 gallons per minute. Most permitted wells serve domestic or household uses, and the records are dominated by unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers rather than Denver Basin formations.

That does not guarantee the same result on every lot. Only 367 wells report total depth, 94 report pump yield, and 80 report static water level. Use these records to frame a drilling bid and investigate a specific parcel, not to treat the nearby median as a promise. Somerset, Hotchkiss, Crawford, Lazear, Cedaredge, and Orchard City provide useful comparison areas, but the closest neighboring wells matter most.

sections.heading: Paonia well depths and the ground below
sections.html:
Paonia’s reported well depth is shallow compared with many Colorado mountain and basin areas. The median is 67 feet, and the middle half runs from 36 to 138 feet. Sixty-three percent of the wells with depth records are under 100 feet, while 34% fall between 100 and 300 feet. The 90th percentile is 212 feet, and the deepest record reaches 640 feet.

For a driller’s bid, that spread matters more than the median alone. A lot near shallow alluvium may be straightforward, while a nearby fractured-bedrock site can require substantially more footage. The permits identify 665 wells in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, compared with 5 alluvial wells and 2 Mesa Verde Group wells. Have the driller review neighboring completions before choosing a target depth.

sections.heading: How much water a Paonia well may produce
sections.html:
Reported yields are strong overall: the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Of the wells that report a pump yield, 54% produce more than 15 gallons per minute, 32% produce between 5 and 15, and 14% produce between 1 and 5.

No reported well in this dataset falls under 1 gallon per minute, but that does not remove the risk of a low-yield result on an untested parcel. Yield records are available for only 94 wells, and a pumping rate is not the same as dependable long-term storage. Ask for the well test, static level, pumping level, recovery information, and permitted use. A household system also needs appropriate pump, tank, and pressure equipment.

sections.heading: Paonia water levels and the decade pattern
sections.html:
The median static water level is 20 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 12 to 66 feet. That is useful for estimating pump placement and trench work, but water levels can vary by location, season, construction, and measurement method.

The decade series does not show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was 11 feet in the 2000s, 48 feet in the 2010s, and 35 feet in the 2020s. The later measurements remain deeper than the 2000s figure, but the 2020s median is shallower than the 2010s median. Treat this as a reason to check current neighboring measurements, not proof that the regional water table is either falling or recovering. A driller should confirm static and pumping levels at the proposed site.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Paonia, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity has continued through the present record, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. The largest decade was the 2000s, with 209 permits. The 1990s had 99, while the 2010s and 2020s each had 80. Earlier records include 8 permits in the 1960s, 38 in the 1970s, and 24 in the 1980s.

The most active names in the records are Wildcat Drilling & Pump, Inc. (Kissner, Billy D.) with 68 wells, Bill Kissner Drilling Inc (Kissner, Bill F.) with 58, and Wildcat Drilling And Pump (Mcpherson, Brian) with 54. These names help identify local experience, but older permit history is not a substitute for a current site review. Confirm licensing, scope, testing, casing, grout, pump work, and who handles the permit before signing.

sections.heading: What a new Paonia well may cost
sections.html:
For Paonia’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, the cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $75 per foot. At the local median depth of 67 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $3,400 to $5,000. That is only the drilling portion, not a complete operating water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,400 to $17,000 at the median depth. The actual bid can move outside that range when the hole must go deeper, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or electrical and trench distances increase. Get the contractor to separate footage, casing, grout, development, testing, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, and permit-related work.

sections.heading: Paonia risks to check before you buy or build
sections.html:
Water quantity is only one part of due diligence. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 42 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those mapped sites do not automatically mean a particular well is contaminated, but they support testing for site-appropriate contaminants and reviewing nearby land uses, mine history, and prior sampling.

Ask for a certified water test and check construction records for casing, grout, and well location. Confirm that the permit allows the intended household, stock, or irrigation use. Septic setbacks, soil conditions, driveway access, building location, and trench routes can determine whether a seemingly shallow well is practical. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed for some uses, so verify water rights with Colorado DWR before building.

sections.heading: Buying land around Paonia: a practical next step
sections.html:
Before closing, collect permits and completion records for the closest neighboring wells, not just averages from Paonia, Hotchkiss, or Somerset. Compare depth, reported yield, static water level, aquifer description, use, and drilling year. The local records are mostly domestic or household wells at 68%, with stock wells at 11%, irrigation at 2%, and monitoring wells at 18%. That mix helps explain the dataset but does not establish your legal water supply.

For a vacant lot, make the well location and drilling plan part of the feasibility review. Have a licensed driller inspect access and estimate a realistic depth range, then coordinate septic and house placement around setbacks and drainage. For an existing home, verify the permit, pump performance, storage, electrical system, recent water quality, and any shared-well agreement. A short records review before purchase can expose a low-yield, contamination, access, or permitting problem early.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Paonia, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Paonia is 67 feet. The middle half runs from 36 to 138 feet, 63% are under 100 feet, and the deepest record reaches 640 feet. Most permits are associated with unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, so neighboring well depths should guide expectations for a particular parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Paonia?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 67-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $3,400 to $5,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,400 to $17,000. Deeper drilling, difficult access, casing, grout, and long utility runs can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Paonia wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 94 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0. Fifty-four percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 14% report 1 to 5. These figures are useful context, but a site-specific pumping and recovery test is still necessary.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Paonia?
faq.a: A Paonia well should be tested rather than assumed safe. The mapped area includes 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 42 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those locations do not prove contamination at your property, but they make a certified test and review of local mine and environmental history important before drinking the water.

faq.q: What should I check before buying a property with a Paonia well?
faq.a: Review the DWR permit, construction record, well depth, yield, static water level, pump condition, water test, and permitted use. Nearby records show a 20-foot median static water level and 68% domestic or household use, but only 80 wells report static levels. Also confirm septic setbacks, access, electrical needs, and whether an augmentation plan is required for the intended use.
